newsitem.title: UK: P&U may not meet profit margin goal.
newsitem.headline: P&U may not meet profit margin goal.

text.p: U.S.-Swedish drugs firm Pharmacia & Upjohn said on Wednesday it may not achieve its goal of a 25 percent operating profit margin by 1998.

In an interview with Reuters, chief financial officer Bob Salisbury said there may be a delay in achieving the target because of planned investments in new products and because of adverse currency movements.
Salisbury added the same factors may affect P&U's aim of achieving $500 million of annual costs savings by 1998 from the 1995 merger between Upjohn from the U.S. and Sweden's Pharmacia.

"We are still on track for those (savings). The issues we have to consider are the impact of foreign exchange that may be detracting somwhat from those as well as the need to possibly invest some of those merger savings in the new product introduction," he said.
P&U plans to invest $150 million in new products and new markets in 1997, but had not yet decided what amount it would set aside for the same purpose in 1998, Salisbury said.
Setting aside the impact of currency movements, Salisbury predicted that P&U earnings will grow in the first-quarter, driven by new produts.
He said P&U was currently reviewing its hedging policy to fight foreign exchange uncertainties and declined to speculate on the outcome.

P&U earlier reported that fourth quarter earnings per share before non-recurring items rose to $0.51 from 0.48. Full-year earnings per share before restructuring and merger costs came in at $1.90, in the middle of analysts' expectations.
Salisbury caused a stir among P&U investors in October when he said that analysts' estimates for 1997 earnings were too high and he stayed clear from making similar comments today.
"Because of the experience we had and the way people reacted to the way we provided guidance...we are going to be a bit less explicit," he said.

"We are going to point people's attention to the uncertainties about foreign exchange and the need to invest in new products and we leave it to them to see if that will resolve to an adjustment of their expectations," Salisbury added.
Back in October, he had said that average market forecasts for 1997 earnings of around $2.35 per share were around 10 cents too high.
P&U's operating profit margin rose to 19.8 percent in 1996 from 18.3 percent the year before.

Speaking of the 25 percent target for 1998, Salisbury said: "We are not setting aside our goal of 25 percent operating marging, but these factors (currency and new products investments) could possibly delay the timing of achieving that."
Earlier, P&U reported that net sales increased to $1.940 billion in 1996 from $1.805 billion.
It added that foreign currency exchange reduced sales by two percentage points in the fourth quarter. Salisbury, however, would not say what the impact had been on profits.

P&U has regularly attracted market doubts over the synergies coming from the merger which created the drugs giant. The company raised more suspicions about the merger's success only last month when it suddenly announced that chief executive John Zabriskie would step down.

But Salisbury said P&U had now left all the merger disruptions behind it. He added that the company was still busy finding a successor for Zabrieski, who has been temporarily replaced by Jan Ekberg, the head of P&U's board.
